S33.supports: Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi publicly rejected the U.S. claim that mines in the Strait of Hormuz had been cleared, calling it a propaganda hoax/deception; he argued that only Iran knows the exact mine locations and said U.S. minesweepers entering the area would be targets.
S33.quality: IRANIAN STATE MEDIA / ACTOR CLAIM; strong for fact of Iran's rebuttal, not for physical mine-state verification

S34.supports: AFP independently reported that Gharibabadi called the U.S. mine-clearance claim 'propaganda deception' and warned that Iran would target U.S. minesweepers entering the area.
S34.quality: HIGH for FACT OF IRANIAN PUBLIC REBUTTAL / THREAT; does not independently verify the physical mine state

S35.supports: Al Jazeera reported that there is no clear public answer on how many mines remain or where they are; Iran has not officially disclosed the minefield. It also reported Gharibabadi's rejection of the U.S. clearance claim and his threat against U.S. mine-detection vessels.
S35.quality: SECONDARY SYNTHESIS; useful for unresolved mine-state context

S36.supports: Iran had earlier published a map showing parts of the Strait that it said were mined and an alternative route for approved ships. The public map identified hazardous/mined geometry at area level rather than publishing a mine-by-mine coordinate ledger.
S36.quality: SECONDARY REPORTING; strong for fact of public area-level map, not proof of exact mine coordinates

S37.supports: U.S. Central Command said the U.S. military eliminated 16 Iranian mine-laying vessels near Hormuz; Trump separately said 10 inactive mine-laying vessels had previously been destroyed, and the Pentagon said it was striking mine-laying vessels and mine-storage facilities.
S37.quality: HIGH for FACT OF U.S./CENTCOM CLAIMS; does not establish total elimination of Iranian minelaying capability

S38.supports: Chatham House assessed that Iran had not publicly confirmed exact mine numbers or precise locations; it distinguished Iran's previously declared hazardous area from suspected individual minefield locations and noted that Iranian participation could still provide information on mine placement, types and arming settings.
S38.quality: CREDIBLE ANALYTIC SECONDARY SOURCE; useful for distinguishing area-level disclosure from exact mine-location knowledge

S39.supports: CENTCOM said USS Frank E. Petersen (DDG-121) and USS Michael Murphy (DDG-112) transited the Strait of Hormuz and operated in the Arabian Gulf as U.S. forces began setting conditions for mine clearance and establishing a new safe passage.
S39.quality: PRIMARY U.S. MILITARY SOURCE; high for fact of announced destroyer transit/mission, not independent proof that every mine threat was absent along the route

S40.supports: Contemporaneous reporting paired the April 11 DDG transit with Iran's April 9 government-approved traffic chart. Critical Threats assessed that the destroyer transit was intended to demonstrate that the normal Traffic Separation Scheme was safe and viable despite Iran's declared hazardous area and mine threat.
S40.quality: CREDIBLE SECONDARY REPORTING / ANALYTIC ASSESSMENT; stronger for chronology and declared purpose than for exact ship track inside every portion of the Iranian hazard polygon

hormuz_update.title: Aug. 26 correction — the U.S. demining claim is openly contested
hormuz_update.text: Washington says U.S. forces removed or detonated the mines in the international waters of Hormuz. Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi publicly rejected that account as propaganda, argued that only Iran knows the exact mine locations, and threatened U.S. minesweepers. That exclusivity claim should be read against earlier public evidence: Iran had already published an area-level map showing mined/hazardous Strait geometry and an alternative approved route; U.S. forces had attacked multiple Iranian mine-laying vessels and mine-storage facilities; and two U.S. guided-missile destroyers publicly transited the Strait on April 11 as part of the mine-clearance/new-passage mission after Iran's April 9 chart was published. Contemporary analysis treated that destroyer transit as an effort to demonstrate that the normal Traffic Separation Scheme remained viable despite Iran's declared mine threat. The current public-source review located no Iranian retraction or correction of the April 9 hazard chart, but absence of a located retraction is not proof that none existed. None of this proves Washington possesses a complete mine-by-mine coordinate and arming ledger, nor that Iran lost all ability to lay new mines. It does, however, materially weaken the claim that the coalition was wholly dependent on Iran for useful minefield knowledge or practical lane testing. The physical completeness of U.S. demining remains independently unresolved, and depressed commercial traffic means a claimed mine-clear lane is not equivalent to restored commercial normalization.

node_evidence.claim: Washington says U.S. forces cleared mines from the international waters of Hormuz; Iran publicly rejects that account as propaganda.
node_evidence.confidence: High that both governments made the claims; independent completeness verification remains unresolved
node_evidence.editorial_note: Do not convert either Washington's clearance claim or Tehran's continued-mine-control claim into independently established physical fact.

node_evidence.claim: Washington is trying to remove mine clearance from Iran's exclusive bargaining leverage while Tehran tries to preserve uncertainty and deterrence around the minefield. Earlier Iranian area-level mine disclosure, U.S. attacks on mine-laying infrastructure, and the April 11 DDG transit after publication of Iran's hazard chart mean Tehran's informational and practical exclusivity was already degraded, though not eliminated.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Iran's public map did not amount to a mine-by-mine coordinate ledger, and destruction of multiple minelayers does not prove total elimination of Iranian laying capacity. Public reporting confirms DDG transit through the Strait and the mission purpose; exact overlap with every part of the Iranian hazard polygon should not be overstated.

node_evidence.claim: Gharibabadi says only Iran knows the precise mine locations and warns that U.S. minesweepers entering the area would be targets.
node_evidence.editorial_note: Treat the claimed exclusive knowledge of precise mine locations as an Iranian assertion. Earlier public disclosure covered broader hazardous/mined areas, not a verified exact mine ledger.

node_evidence.claim: Before the current demining dispute, Iran publicly identified mined/hazardous Strait geometry and an alternative approved route; U.S. forces had struck numerous Iranian mine-laying vessels and mine-storage facilities; and DDG-121 and DDG-112 then transited the Strait on April 11 as part of the U.S. mine-clearance/new-passage mission.
node_evidence.confidence: High for the public map, U.S. strike claims, and announced DDG transit; lower for the remaining fraction of Iranian minelaying capability and exact destroyer track relative to every portion of the declared hazard area
node_evidence.editorial_note: No Iranian retraction/correction of the April 9 hazard chart was located in the Aug. 26 public-source review. Treat that as a search result, not proof of universal absence. This context weakens claims of complete Iranian informational or operational exclusivity without proving exact U.S. knowledge of every mine or eliminating Iran's ability to re-mine the Strait.
